title: Defensive programming
locators: CC8 (Code Complete 2nd ed. ch. 8 'Defensive Programming'); SW4.4 (SWEBOK Guide V4.0 ch. 4 'Software Construction' §4.4; its V3 counterpart, ch. 3 §4.4 'Assertions, Design by Contract, and Defensive Programming', is openable in the ligurio/swebok-v3 transcription master 3_software_construction.md)
candidate_evidence: Casalnuovo, Devanbu, Oliveira, Filkov, Ray, 'Assert use in GitHub projects' (ICSE 2015) — asserts and defect occurrence in C and C++ projects

Osman, Leuenberger, Lungu, Nierstrasz, 'Tracking null checks in open-source Java systems' (SANER 2016, DOI 10.1109/SANER.2016.57) — 810 systems; 35% of conditional statements contain null checks; null returned to signal errors instead of an exception

Estler, Furia, Nordio, Piccioni, Meyer, 'Contracts in practice' (FM 2014, LNCS 8442; arXiv 1211.4775) — which contract elements, preconditions among them, developers write in 21 Eiffel, C# and Java projects

tool rules on unchecked dereference: SpotBugs NP_NULL_ON_SOME_PATH and the NP_* family (spotbugs/spotbugs master spotbugs/etc/messages.xml), PMD AvoidCatchingNPE (pmd/pmd pmd-java category/java/errorprone.xml), typescript-eslint no-non-null-assertion (packages/eslint-plugin/docs/rules/no-non-null-assertion.mdx), go vet nilness (golang/tools go/analysis/passes/nilness/doc.go); SonarSource java S2259 'Null pointers should not be dereferenced' — the source-map path java-checks/.../rules/java/S2259.html answered 404 on 2026-09-27, so the current RSPEC path must be located first

tool rules on checks that abort or vanish: clippy unwrap_used and expect_used (rust-lang/rust-clippy clippy_lints/src/methods/mod.rs) and indexing_slicing (clippy_lints/src/indexing_slicing.rs); Ruff S101 assert (astral-sh/ruff crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/flake8_bandit/rules/assert_used.rs — assertions are removed when Python runs with optimization)

official documentation on argument checks: Objects.requireNonNull javadoc (openjdk/jdk jdk-21-ga src/java.base/share/classes/java/util/Objects.java), Guava Preconditions javadoc (google/guava master guava/src/com/google/common/base/Preconditions.java), Rust API guidelines C-VALIDATE 'Functions validate their arguments' (rust-lang/api-guidelines master src/dependability.md)

official documentation on failing fast versus recovering: Rust book ch. 9 'To panic! or Not to panic!' (rust-lang/book main src/ch09-03-to-panic-or-not-to-panic.md — guidelines for error handling, custom types for validation), CPython language reference 'The assert statement' (python/cpython Doc/reference/simple_stmts.rst — __debug__ and -O), Effective Go 'Panic' and 'Recover' (golang/website _content/doc/effective_go.html)

SWEBOK V3 ch. 3 §4.4 'Assertions, Design by Contract, and Defensive Programming' (ligurio/swebok-v3 master 3_software_construction.md) as the openable counterpart of SW4.4; the SWEBOK V4.0 text itself is not openable
notes: Owns the defensive stance inside the trust boundary: checking a routine's preconditions (null, range, state) on entry and failing fast at the point of violation rather than continuing with bad data, the choice between failing and substituting a value when a check fails, an internal barricade between checked entry points and the code that trusts them, forced unwraps and unchecked dereferences, checks that vanish in optimized builds, and how much debugging aid stays in production code. Yields validation of a value that crosses a trust boundary to security-hygiene-in-ordinary-code; the statement of preconditions, postconditions and invariants as a contract, and the assertion as specification, to contracts-assertions-and-invariants (which shares CC8 and SW4.4); the local catching, wrapping and propagating of a failure to error-and-exception-handling; a retried or timed-out remote call to fault-tolerance-retries-timeouts-fallbacks. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a rule that holds in one language belongs elsewhere, so a check is 'the language's precondition check or assertion', never one language's keyword. Security-critical design and concurrency correctness are reserved specialties outside the corpus: the topic stops at ordinary checks inside the trust boundary and covers neither threat modelling nor race-free checking.

title: Fault tolerance with retries, timeouts and fallbacks
locators: SW4.5 (SWEBOK Guide V4.0 ch. 4 'Software Construction' §4.5; its V3 counterpart, ch. 3 §4.5 'Error Handling, Exception Handling, and Fault Tolerance', is openable in the ligurio/swebok-v3 transcription master 3_software_construction.md); the call-site discipline is usually formulated in practice from the stability patterns of Nygard's Release It! (2nd ed.) and the Google SRE book chapter 'Addressing Cascading Failures' — practitioner texts, formulation only
candidate_evidence: Gunawi et al., 'Why does the cloud stop computing? Lessons from hundreds of service outages' (SoCC 2016) — 597 unplanned outages; missing or incorrect failure detection and buggy failover code

Dai, He, Gu, Lu, 'Understanding real-world timeout problems in cloud server systems' (IC2E 2018) — 156 timeout bugs in 11 cloud server systems; misused timeout values and missing timeout checking dominate

Stoica, Sethi, Su, Zhou, Lu, Mace, Musuvathi, Nath, 'If at first you don't succeed, try, try, again...? Insights and LLM-informed tooling for detecting retry bugs in software systems' (SOSP 2024, DOI 10.1145/3694715.3695971) — retry is hard to implement and test; the Wasabi toolkit

Bronson, Aghayev, Charapko, Zhu, 'Metastable failures in distributed systems' (HotOS 2021, DOI 10.1145/3458336.3465286) — bears only on the call-site rule of bounded retries with backoff (retry amplification), not on system design

tool rules on missing timeouts: Pylint W3101 missing-timeout (pylint-dev/pylint pylint/checkers/method_args.py), Ruff S113 request-without-timeout (astral-sh/ruff crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/flake8_bandit/rules/request_without_timeout.rs), Semgrep use-timeout (semgrep/semgrep-rules develop python/requests/best-practice/use-timeout.yaml)

official documentation on deadlines and retries: Go net/http Client.Timeout 'A Timeout of zero means no timeout' (golang/go src/net/http/client.go) and the context package's deadlines and cancellation (src/context/context.go); Python asyncio.timeout (python/cpython Doc/library/asyncio-task.rst); gRPC deadlines and retry guides (grpc/grpc.io main content/en/docs/guides/deadlines.md and retry.md) and the client-retry design A6 (grpc/proposal master A6-client-retries.md)

standards on idempotency: IETF draft 'The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field' (ietf-wg-httpapi/idempotency main draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header.md); RFC 9110 §9.2.2 'Idempotent Methods' and §10.2.3 'Retry-After' (httpwg/http-core — the draft path under main did not resolve on 2026-09-27; rfc-editor.org is not openable)
SWEBOK V3 ch. 3 §4.5 'Error Handling, Exception Handling, and Fault Tolerance' (ligurio/swebok-v3 master 3_software_construction.md) as the openable counterpart of SW4.5

the AWS Builders' Library article 'Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter' is not openable (aws.amazon.com denied) and the Google SRE book is not openable (sre.google is not an admitted host); both are formulation at best, never a card's anchor
notes: Owns the discipline at the call site of a remote or otherwise blocking operation: a bounded timeout or deadline on every such call and its propagation to callees, retrying only a failure that is transient, with a bounded attempt count and backoff with jitter, retrying only an operation that is idempotent or made so with an idempotency key, retrying at one layer rather than at every layer, and a fallback that is explicit and observable rather than a silent default that masks the failure. Yields the local handling of a failure (catch, wrap, propagate, clean up) to error-and-exception-handling; preconditions and fail-fast inside the trust boundary to defensive-programming; the release of the connection or handle to resource-management-and-ownership; the log record of a retry or fallback to logging-and-diagnostic-output; timeout and retry values as settings to runtime-configuration. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a rule that holds in one language belongs elsewhere, and a client library's name may appear in an Example only. Distributed-systems design (replication, consensus, service topology, load shedding, circuit-breaker architecture across services) and middleware are outside the corpus and concurrency correctness is a reserved specialty, so the rules stop at the call site's retry, timeout, idempotency and fallback discipline.

title: Resource management and ownership
locators: PP 'How to Balance Resources' (The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th anniversary ed., ch. 4 'Pragmatic Paranoia', topic 26: finish what you start, act locally, deallocate in the opposite order of allocation)
candidate_evidence: Weimer, Necula, 'Finding and preventing run-time error handling mistakes' (OOPSLA 2004, DOI 10.1145/1028976.1029011) — over 800 mistakes in almost 4 million lines of Java from failing to release resources or clean up along all paths

Kellogg, Shadab, Sridharan, Ernst, 'Lightweight and modular resource leak verification' (ESEC/FSE 2021, DOI 10.1145/3468264.3468576) — leak checking as accumulation analysis with lightweight ownership transfer; 49 real resource leaks

Ghanavati, Costa, Seboek, Lo, Andrzejak, 'Memory and resource leak defects and their repairs in Java projects' (EMSE 2020, DOI 10.1007/s10664-019-09731-8; arXiv 1810.00101) — 491 issues in 15 Java projects; most leaks manifest on error-free execution paths

tool rules on Java resources: PMD CloseResource (pmd/pmd pmd-java category/java/errorprone.xml), SpotBugs OBL_UNSATISFIED_OBLIGATION and OS_OPEN_STREAM (spotbugs/spotbugs master spotbugs/etc/messages.xml), Error Prone MustBeClosedChecker (google/error-prone master docs/bugpattern/MustBeClosedChecker.md); SonarSource java S2095 'Resources should be closed' — the source-map RSPEC path answered 404 on 2026-09-27

tool rules elsewhere: Pylint R1732 consider-using-with (pylint-dev/pylint pylint/checkers/refactoring/refactoring_checker.py), Ruff SIM115 open-file-with-context-handler (astral-sh/ruff crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/flake8_simplify/rules/open_file_with_context_handler.rs), go vet lostcancel (golang/tools go/analysis/passes/lostcancel/doc.go)

official documentation on scoped release in garbage-collected languages: AutoCloseable javadoc (openjdk/jdk jdk-21-ga src/java.base/share/classes/java/lang/AutoCloseable.java); PEP 343 'The "with" Statement' (python/peps main peps/pep-0343.rst) and contextlib (python/cpython Doc/library/contextlib.rst); Effective Go 'Defer' (golang/website _content/doc/effective_go.html); the Java Language Specification §14.20.3 try-with-resources is not openable

official documentation and standards on ownership and explicit disposal: Rust book ch. 4 'What Is Ownership?' (rust-lang/book main src/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.md) and ch. 15 'Running Code on Cleanup with the Drop Trait' (src/ch15-03-drop.md); TC39 Explicit Resource Management proposal (tc39/proposal-explicit-resource-management main README.md) and the TypeScript 5.2 release notes on using declarations (microsoft/TypeScript-Website v2 packages/documentation/copy/en/release-notes/TypeScript 5.2.md)
notes: Owns the lifetime of a non-memory resource (file, socket, connection, stream, cancellation function, temporary file) and its ownership: the routine or object that acquires a resource releases it, through the language's scoped-release construct rather than by hand; release happens on every path, the exceptional ones included; resources are released in the opposite order of acquisition; each resource has one owner at a time and a transfer of ownership is explicit in the interface; finalizers and garbage collection are not relied on to release a non-memory resource. Yields the catch-and-propagate structure around the release to error-and-exception-handling; shared mutable state between components to mutable-state-and-immutability; memory use and pooling for speed to profiling-and-code-tuning; a connection's timeout and retry to fault-tolerance-retries-timeouts-fallbacks. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a rule that holds in one language belongs elsewhere, so a rule names 'the language's scoped-release construct' and the applies_to traits garbage-collected and manual-memory separate what differs. Concurrency correctness (locks, lock ordering, deadlock, release across threads) and low-latency tuning are reserved specialties outside the corpus; the topic stops at single-owner acquire-and-release discipline.

title: Logging and diagnostic output
locators: no canon chapter; researched from the evidence layer. The topic is usually formulated from practitioner texts: The Twelve-Factor App, factor XI 'Logs' (heroku/12factor master content/en/logs.md, openable), the 97 Things essay 'Verbose Logging Will Disturb Your Sleep' (97-things/97-things-every-programmer-should-know master en/thing_90/README.md, openable), and Nygard's Release It! (2nd ed.) on logs in production — formulation only; the Python Logging HOWTO's 'When to use logging' is official documentation and belongs to the evidence layer
candidate_evidence: Yuan, Park, Zhou, 'Characterizing logging practices in open-source software' (ICSE 2012) — four large open-source systems; logging is pervasive and log messages are revised often

Fu, Zhu, Hu, Lou, Ding, Lin, Zhang, Xie, 'Where do developers log? An empirical study on logging practices in industry' (ICSE SEIP 2014, DOI 10.1145/2591062.2591175) — two Microsoft systems of 2.5M and 10.4M LOC and a survey of 54 developers
Chen, Jiang, 'Characterizing and detecting anti-patterns in the logging code' (ICSE 2017, DOI 10.1109/ICSE.2017.15) — how-to-log anti-patterns and the LCAnalyzer detector

Hassani, Shang, Shihab, Tsantalis, 'Studying and detecting log-related issues' (EMSE 2018, DOI 10.1007/s10664-018-9603-z) — missing or outdated log information; files with log-related issues had more prior changes and bug fixes

tool rules on message construction: Pylint logging checker W1201 logging-not-lazy and W1203 logging-fstring-interpolation (pylint-dev/pylint pylint/checkers/logging.py), Ruff flake8-logging-format G rules (astral-sh/ruff crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/flake8_logging_format/violations.rs), PMD GuardLogStatement (pmd/pmd pmd-java category/java/bestpractices.xml), go vet printf (golang/tools go/analysis/passes/printf/doc.go — format strings of Printf-style log calls)

tool rules on console output in place of a logging facility: ESLint no-console (eslint/eslint main docs/src/rules/no-console.md), clippy print_stdout and print_stderr (rust-lang/rust-clippy clippy_lints/src/write/mod.rs)

official documentation: CPython Logging HOWTO (python/cpython Doc/howto/logging.rst — when to use logging, the levels), Go log/slog package doc (golang/go src/log/slog/doc.go — structured records and levels), Rust log crate README (rust-lang/log master README.md — libraries use the facade, executables choose the implementation)

standards: OpenTelemetry logs data model (open-telemetry/opentelemetry-specification main specification/logs/data-model.md — severity number ranges), OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet (OWASP/CheatSheetSeries master cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.md — data to exclude), OWASP ASVS 5.0 V16 'Security Logging and Error Handling' (OWASP/ASVS master 5.0/en/0x25-V16-Security-Logging-and-Error-Handling.md); RFC 5424 severity levels are not openable (rfc-editor.org denied, no GitHub source in the source map)
notes: Owns the log and diagnostic statements in ordinary code: whether an event warrants a record, the level that matches its severity, the content a reader needs to act (what failed, with which identifiers and cause, the exception with its stack trace), logging a failure once where it is handled rather than at every layer it passes, parameterized or lazy formatting rather than building a message the level discards, structured fields rather than values spliced into prose, the logging facility rather than print or console output, and diagnostic output to standard error rather than standard output. Yields the decision to catch, wrap or propagate to error-and-exception-handling; a secret or personal datum written to a log to security-hygiene-in-ordinary-code; log-level settings to runtime-configuration; temporary tracing while hunting a bug to debugging; the record of a retry or fallback keeps its content rule here while the retry itself belongs to fault-tolerance-retries-timeouts-fallbacks. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a rule that holds in one language belongs elsewhere, and a logging library's name may appear in an Example only. Security-critical design (audit trails, tamper-evident logs) is a reserved specialty, and log pipelines, distributed tracing and observability platforms belong to distributed systems and middleware, which are outside the corpus; the topic stops at the statement in the code.

title: Unit testing and test quality
locators: CC22 (Code Complete 2nd ed. ch. 22 'Developer Testing'); SEG12 (Software Engineering at Google ch. 12 'Unit Testing': test via public APIs, test state not interactions, test behaviors not methods, don't put logic in tests, write clear failure messages, DAMP not DRY); the 97 Things essays 'Test Precisely and Concretely' (thing_81) and 'Write Tests for People' (thing_95)
candidate_evidence: Bavota, Qusef, Oliveto, De Lucia, Binkley, 'Are test smells really harmful? An empirical study' (Empirical Software Engineering 20(4), 2015) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'high diffusion of test smells in both open source and industrial software systems with 86% of JUnit tests exhibiting at least one test smell'; 'test smells have a strong negative impact on program comprehension and maintenance, with comprehension being 30% better in the absence of test smells' — result list named arxiv.org/pdf/2003.05613 (a later survey citing it) and iris.unisa.it/handle/11386/4465858

Spadini, Palomba, Zaidman, Bruntink, Bacchelli, 'On the relation of test smells to software code quality' (ICSME 2018) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'data on 221 releases of ten software systems and analyzing more than a million test cases'; '(i) tests with smells are more change- and defect-prone, (ii) Indirect Testing, Eager Test, and Assertion Roulette are the most significant smells for change-proneness, and (iii) production code is more defect-prone when tested by smelly tests' — https://pure.tudelft.nl/ws/files/46651094/main.pdf (author copy), https://zenodo.org/record/1689875

Inozemtseva, Holmes, 'Coverage is not strongly correlated with test suite effectiveness' (ICSE 2014) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: '31,000 test suites for five systems consisting of up to 724,000 lines of source code'; 'low to moderate correlation between coverage and effectiveness when the number of test cases in the suite is controlled for'; 'stronger forms of coverage do not provide greater insight into the effectiveness of the suite'; 'coverage, while useful for identifying under-tested parts of a program, should not be used as a quality target' — https://cs.ubc.ca/~rtholmes/papers/icse_2014_inozemtseva.pdf (author copy); a neverworkintheory.org review exists (2021/09/24/coverage-is-not-strongly-correlated-with-test-suite-effectiveness.html, GitHub-hosted source)

tool rules on JVM tests: PMD UnitTestShouldIncludeAssert, UnitTestContainsTooManyAsserts and UnitTestAssertionsShouldIncludeMessage (pmd/pmd pmd-java category/java/bestpractices.xml; the JUnit* names before PMD 7), Error Prone JUnit4TestNotRun and AssertionFailureIgnored (google/error-prone master docs/bugpattern/*.md); SonarSource java S2699 'Tests should include assertions' — the source-map RSPEC path answered 404 on 2026-09-27

tool rules elsewhere: eslint-plugin-jest expect-expect and no-conditional-expect (jest-community/eslint-plugin-jest main docs/rules/*.md), Ruff flake8-pytest-style PT018 composite assertion (astral-sh/ruff crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/flake8_pytest_style/rules/assertion.rs), go vet tests (golang/tools go/analysis/passes/tests/doc.go)

official framework documentation: CPython unittest (python/cpython Doc/library/unittest.rst), pytest 'How to write and report assertions in tests' (pytest-dev/pytest main doc/en/how-to/assert.rst), Rust book ch. 11 'How to Write Tests' (rust-lang/book main src/ch11-01-writing-tests.md), Go blog 'Using Subtests and Sub-benchmarks' on table-driven tests (golang/website _content/blog/subtests.md)
review guidance: google/eng-practices master review/reviewer/looking-for.md, section 'Tests' — tests are correct, sensible and useful, fail when the code is broken, make simple and useful assertions
notes: Owns the test's own assertion and structure: one behaviour per test with a name that states it, the arrange-act-assert shape, assertions that check the outcome precisely and fail when the code is broken (no assertion-free test, no assertion roulette, no assertion inside a condition, no swallowed assertion failure), no branching or loop logic in a test, testing through the public interface rather than private internals, independence from execution order and shared state, descriptive duplication over abstraction in test code, and coverage as a pointer to untested code rather than a target. Yields a test that mocks what it should not, and the choice of fake, stub or mock, to test-doubles; tests against real dependencies and their flakiness to larger-tests-integration-and-end-to-end; generated inputs to property-based-testing; the order of writing tests and code to test-first-and-test-driven-development; tests that pin existing behaviour before a change to seams-and-characterization-tests. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a rule that holds in one language belongs elsewhere, and a test framework's name may appear in an Example only. Concurrency correctness is a reserved specialty: a test of thread interleavings is outside the corpus.

title: Test-first and test-driven development
locators: SW4.16 (SWEBOK Guide V4.0 ch. 4 'Software Construction' §4.16; its V3 counterpart, ch. 3 §4.16 'Test-First Programming', is openable in the ligurio/swebok-v3 transcription master 3_software_construction.md); PP 'Test to Code' (The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th anniversary ed., ch. 7 'While You Are Coding', topic 41); johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code main README.md §'Test-Driven Development' and §'TDD Summary' (the public discussion of the two positions); Beck, Test-Driven Development: By Example, as the formulation the discipline side follows (trade book, never evidence)

(IEEE TSE 2017; arXiv 1611.05994) — 82 data points from 39 professionals; granularity and uniformity of the cycle are associated with quality and productivity, sequencing has no important influence

Nagappan, Maximilien, Bhat, Williams, 'Realizing quality improvement through test driven development: results and experiences of four industrial teams' (EMSE 2008, 13(3):289–302) — three Microsoft teams and one IBM team; pre-release defect density 40–90% lower than similar projects without TDD; 15–35% more initial development time, reported subjectively
official documentation on the discipline side: the Rust book's test-driven walk-through in ch. 12 (rust-lang/book main src/ch12-04-testing-the-librarys-functionality.md)

review guidance on the tests-with-the-change side: google/eng-practices master review/reviewer/looking-for.md, section 'Tests' — tests are added in the same change as the production code, with no order prescribed
SWEBOK V3 ch. 3 §4.16 'Test-First Programming' (ligurio/swebok-v3 master 3_software_construction.md) as the openable counterpart of SW4.16

Fucci, Scanniello, Romano, Shepperd, Sigweni, Uyaguari, Turhan, Juristo, Oivo, 'An external replication on the effects of test-driven development using a multi-site blind analysis approach' (ESEM 2016) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: a crossover replication with 21 graduate students at the University of Basilicata with blind analysis at UPM and Brunel; Kruskal–Wallis tests showed no significant difference between TDD and test-last in testing effort (p = .27), external code quality (p = .82) or productivity (p = .83) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2961111.2962592 (author copy https://people.brunel.ac.uk/~csstmms/FucciEtAl_ESEM2016.pdf)

Nagappan, Maximilien, Bhat, Williams, 'Realizing quality improvement through test driven development: results and experiences of four industrial teams' (EMSE 13(3), 2008) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: case studies of three Microsoft teams and one IBM team; pre-release defect density decreased between 40% and 90% relative to similar projects not using TDD, at a 15–35% increase in initial development time — a PDF copy is hosted on GitHub at tpn/pdfs (raw.githubusercontent.com/tpn/pdfs/master/Realizing%20Quality%20Improvement%20Through%20Test%20Driven%20Development%20-%20Results%20and%20Experiences%20of%20Four%20Industrial%20Teams%20(nagappan_tdd).pdf)

Karac, Turhan, 'What do we (really) know about test-driven development?' (IEEE Software 35(4), 2018) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: an analysis of the TDD studies arguing the evidence that TDD beats another development method is not strong — https://www.cse.unr.edu/~dascalus/Paper_JAMES.pdf

Tosun, Dieste, Fucci, Vegas, Turhan, Erdogmus, Santos, Oivo, Toro, Jarvinen, Juristo, 'An industry experiment on the effects of test-driven development on external quality and productivity' (EMSE 22, 2017) — relayed by the orchestrator's search — https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s10664-016-9490-0.pdf

Santos, Vegas, Dieste, Uyaguari, Tosun, Fucci, Turhan, Scanniello, Romano, Karac, Kuhrmann, Mandić, Ramač, Pfahl, Engblom, Kyykka, Rungi, Palomäki, Spisak, Oivo, Juristo, 'A family of experiments on test-driven development' (EMSE 26, 2021; arXiv:2011.11942) — relayed by the orchestrator's search — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.11942

Fucci, Romano, Baldassarre, Caivano, Scanniello, Turhan, Juristo, 'A longitudinal cohort study on the retainment of test-driven development' (ESEM 2018) and Baldassarre et al., 'Studying test-driven development and its retainment over a six-month time span' (JSS 2021; arXiv:2105.03312) — relayed by the orchestrator's search (arXiv id confirmed in the result list) — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.03312

Ghafari, Gross, Fucci, Felderer, 'Why research on test-driven development is inconclusive?' (ESEM 2020; arXiv:2007.09863) — relayed by the orchestrator's search (arXiv id confirmed in the result list) — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.09863
notes: Owns the order and cadence of writing tests relative to production code: writing a failing test before the code that makes it pass, the size and uniformity of the test-code-refactor cycle, and the alternative in which a small unit of code is written first and its unit tests follow before the code counts as working. Yields assertion quality and test structure to unit-testing-and-test-quality; the choice of double to test-doubles; the refactor step's technique to refactoring; the size of one change to small-steps-and-minimal-diffs. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a rule that holds in one language belongs elsewhere. The topic is contested: Robert C. Martin (Clean Code) holds TDD as a discipline, the three laws and the Red-Green-Refactor loop, in his reply under §'Test-Driven Development' of the johnousterhout/aposd-vs-clean-code README, while John Ousterhout (A Philosophy of Software Design) holds that 'bundling', writing a few tens to a few hundred lines of code and then their unit tests, serves equally, in his opening of that section and in §'TDD Summary', where both agree unit tests are essential and disagree on TDD's average and worst-case outcomes. The evidence layer is the controlled-experiment and industrial-case-study literature; Fucci et al. find sequencing without important influence and cycle granularity and uniformity associated with quality and productivity, a candidate separating condition for §Contested rules. No static-analysis rule checks whether a test preceded the code, so the tool channel carries nothing for the ordering claim. Team adoption of TDD as a process is process and team management, outside the corpus; the topic keeps the individual developer's working order.

notes: Owns tests that exercise more than one unit against real or high-fidelity dependencies: the size and scope of a test and the balance between many small tests and few large ones, hermetic environments and test data that each test creates and removes, waiting on a condition rather than on elapsed time, isolating and diagnosing flakiness, and keeping slow tests selectable apart from the fast suite. Yields the assertion and structure of each test to unit-testing-and-test-quality; the choice of fake, stub or mock in place of a real dependency to test-doubles; the CI pipeline that runs the suites to build-warnings-static-analysis-ci; tests pinned around legacy code before a change to seams-and-characterization-tests. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a rule that holds in one language belongs elsewhere, and a browser-automation or container tool's name may appear in an Example only. Distributed-systems testing (fault injection across services, chaos experiments), cross-platform device matrices and UX acceptance decisions are outside the corpus, and load testing for latency belongs to the reserved low-latency specialty.

notes: Owns tests that state a property over generated inputs rather than single examples: choosing properties (round trip, invariant, equivalence with a simpler oracle or model, metamorphic relation, idempotence), generators that produce valid inputs by construction rather than by discarding, shrinking to a minimal counterexample, reproducing a failure from its seed or saved example and keeping it as a regression case, and bounding the run so the suite stays deterministic in CI. Yields the assertion and structure of example-based tests to unit-testing-and-test-quality; doubles to test-doubles; the contract a property restates to contracts-assertions-and-invariants. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a rule that holds in one language belongs elsewhere, and a framework's name may appear in an Example only. No static-analysis rule checks property quality; the frameworks' runtime health checks are the nearest tool evidence. Machine-learning or algorithm research (search-based test generation, fuzzing research) and concurrency correctness (linearizability checking) are reserved specialties outside the corpus.
